justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift from what I assumed was a current price near 1018–1020, with the 1-day estimate essentially anchoring near the prevailing level given how little tends to change in a single session under normal conditions. The 1-week estimate nudges slightly higher to 1022, reflecting a mild bullish bias that could stem from prevailing trend momentum, mean-reversion tendencies, or a slightly positive carry environment depending on the underlying asset in question. The 1-month estimate of 1035 extends that gradual drift further, consistent with a low-volatility regime where prices trend slowly upward without dramatic reversals. In each case, I was essentially projecting a continuation of recent conditions rather than anticipating a sharp regime change.

The confidence interval widths widen substantially as the horizon extends, which is a standard reflection of uncertainty compounding over time. At the 1-day horizon, a 47-point range (995–1042) suggests I expected relatively contained intraday or overnight volatility, perhaps consistent with an annualized volatility in the 15–25% range depending on the asset. By one week, the interval opens to 95 points, and by one month it reaches 195 points, capturing the realistic possibility that a trending move, volatility spike, or macro surprise could carry the price meaningfully away from the starting point. The asymmetry in the monthly interval — roughly 95 points of downside versus 100 points of upside — reflects a near-symmetric but very slightly positively skewed view.

Key sources of uncertainty include macroeconomic data releases, central bank communications, and liquidity conditions, all of which can shift sentiment and positioning rapidly. Geopolitical shocks, earnings surprises if this is an equity-linked instrument, or sudden changes in commodity supply dynamics could also drive outsized moves. The intervals implicitly assume no catastrophic tail event, so a major financial shock, a sudden policy reversal, or a structural break in the market could easily push outcomes outside the stated 90% confidence bounds.

It is worth noting that my stated intervals represent a 90% confidence range, meaning I explicitly acknowledged a 10% probability that the price falls outside those bounds. In practice, financial return distributions tend to have fat tails, meaning actual extreme outcomes occur more frequently than a normal distribution would suggest. If realized volatility turns out to be higher than my implicit assumption — or if there is a correlated macro shock that affects many assets simultaneously — the tails could be meaningfully heavier than what my intervals imply.
